response.text: Accrual accounting records income when you earn it and expenses when you incur them — not when cash moves. So if you sell something in December but get paid in January, accrual books show the sale in December. Cash-basis accounting records income only when you receive payment and expenses only when you pay them. Cash basis is simpler and can make short-term cash tracking easier; accrual gives a clearer picture of ongoing performance and obligations because it matches income with the costs that created it. Accrual is commonly used for formal financial reporting and by larger businesses, while many small businesses use cash basis when tax rules allow. Which method is right depends on your size, reporting needs, and tax rules — check with your accountant. Sources: IRS Publication 538 (Accounting Periods and Methods); FASB / U.S. GAAP guidance on accrual accounting.
